articles.title: Seoul’s Hangang River recorded 2,062 species in 2022, up from 1,608 in 2007, as the city restored riverbanks and expanded wildlife habitats
articles.summary: Seoul’s Hangang River recorded 2,062 species in 2022, up from 1,608 in 2007, according to the Seoul Metropolitan Government, as restoration projects
articles.body: Seoul’s Hangang River recorded 2,062 species in 2022, up from 1,608 in 2007, according to the Seoul Metropolitan Government, as restoration projects sought to expand wildlife habitats along its banks. The city’s efforts included replacing concrete riverbank structures with natural materials such as soil, gravel and rock, alongside improvements to ecological parks and riverside forests. By 2022, 46.9 kilometres of riverbank sections designated for natural protection had been restored, the government reported. The wider programme also included tree planting and habitat improvements intended to support biodiversity and encourage coexistence between urban residents and wildlife.How did Hangang River restoration boost biodiversityThe city’s restoration plans included replacing concrete and other artificial riverbank structures with natural materials such as soil, gravel and rock. According to the Seoul Metropolitan Government, these natural revetments were intended not only to change the appearance of the riverbanks but also to restore wildlife habitat. Soil and rocks would form bottomlands and provide habitats, while wooden poles would offer resting places for birds.The government also outlined plans to place mats made from plants such as Amur silver grass and Chinese fountain grass along the riverbanks. These measures were intended to support the development of a more natural river ecosystem and increase biodiversity. The city stated that the use of natural materials would help restore the river ecosystem and enhance the surrounding landscape while creating an environment in which people and nature could coexist.How did Seoul restore 46.9 kilometres of Hangang River banksThe Seoul Metropolitan Government reported that the combined length of the Hangang River’s northern and southern banks was 82 kilometres. Of this, 57.1 kilometres had been designated for conversion to natural bank protection, excluding sections where restoration was not possible because of structures such as wharves and bridges. By 2022, 46.9 kilometres of the planned sections had been completed, representing approximately 82% of the designated restoration work.The city’s announcement set out further restoration plans for the remaining sections. These included work near the confluence of Hongjecheon Stream, Seongsandaegyo Bridge and Mangwon Hangang Park, as well as a section between Seonam Water Recycling Centre and Gayangdaegyo Bridge in Gangseo Hangang Park. The government stated that the remaining 6.2 kilometres were scheduled for restoration by 2025, with the overall objective of replacing eligible artificial riverbank protection with natural materials.Seoul to restore Hangang’s ecological parksThe restoration programme also covered five Hangang Ecological Parks: Yeouido Saetgang, Gangseo Wetland, Godeok Waterfront, Amsa and Nanji. The Seoul Metropolitan Government said these parks had different ecological conditions, with some areas showing ecological stability while others experienced interference between public access and wildlife habitats or reduced stability because of intermittent flooding. The city planned to assess each park and tailor improvements to its conditions, including separating public spaces from sensitive ecological areas and planting suitable species in locations affected by flooding.Tree planting was another part of the city’s wider plans for the river. The government reported that the number of trees in Hangang Parks rose from 850,000 in 2005 to 2.06 million in 2011 following the Hangang Renaissance Project. By 2022, approximately 3.5 million trees were present in the parks, according to the city. The government’s subsequent plan aimed to increase that total to 3.71 million trees by 2025. articles.body: A California man has been charged with murdering his estranged wife after her burned remains were found in El Dorado County, with investigators saying he falsely claimed that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents had taken her into custody.Gurinder Gill, 28, was arrested on October 14 and booked into the Sacramento County Main Jail on a murder charge, the Sacramento County Sheriff's Office said.His wife, Jasmine Gill, 30, was last seen at their Sacramento residence on September 30. articles.title: An Ontario farmer says he turned down a C$16 million offer for his 164-acre fruit farm; instead, his family placed 29 acres under a 999-year easement, with plans to protect the rest from development
articles.summary: When a developer offered Charles Stevens C$16 million for Wilmot Orchards, the 164-acre fruit farm he helped build near Newcastle, Ontario, he had every
articles.body: When a developer offered Charles Stevens C$16 million for Wilmot Orchards, the 164-acre fruit farm he helped build near Newcastle, Ontario, he had every reason to consider it. The property sits close to Highway 401 and Lake Ontario, in a rapidly growing part of the Greater Toronto Area where farmland is increasingly attractive for housing and other development. Instead, Stevens and his family chose a very different path. They worked with the Ontario Farmland Trust to place a conservation easement on 29 acres of the farm, legally restricting development for 999 years, and they plan to protect the remaining land in the years ahead. The story has been reported by CBC News, while the Ontario Farmland Trust describes Wilmot Orchards as the first farm in Durham Region protected through its farmland protection programme.The decision was not simply about refusing money. It was about deciding what kind of future the land should have. Wilmot Orchards grows apples and blueberries on some of Canada’s most productive soil, and the Stevens family wanted to ensure that the farm could continue producing food long after the current generation. Their choice turns a private family property into a long-term public commitment to local food, agricultural land and the possibility that future farmers may still afford to work the soil.A farm built over generationsCharles Stevens bought the land that became Wilmot Orchards in 1975, before graduating from the University of Guelph in 1976. Over the decades, the farm became known for its pick-your-own blueberries as well as its apple orchards, drawing thousands of visitors each summer to pick fruit and spend time in the countryside. Today, it remains both a working farm and a community destination, with the next generation of the Stevens family involved in its operation.The farm occupies Class 1 soil, which the Ontario Farmland Trust identifies as Canada’s most fertile and rarest farmland. Only 0.5 percent of Canada’s landmass is considered Class 1, and more than half of that land is in Ontario. That makes the preservation of places such as Wilmot Orchards especially significant, because the same qualities that make the land excellent for growing food also make it desirable for development.Stevens has watched that pressure grow steadily. The farm’s location, about an hour from Toronto, has brought repeated interest from developers hoping to convert agricultural land into non-farm uses. In interviews and public remarks, he has acknowledged that development is not inherently wrong, but argued that Ontario needs to be smarter about where it builds, particularly when construction threatens scarce high-quality farmland.What a 999-year easement meansA conservation easement is a legal agreement attached to the title of a property. It does not necessarily transfer ownership of the land, but it permanently limits certain future uses, in this case preventing the land from being developed for non-agricultural purposes. By placing an easement on Wilmot Orchards, the Stevens family has removed much of the property’s speculative development value while keeping it available for farming.The Ontario Farmland Trust says the family has protected nearly 29 acres of the 164-acre property so far, with plans to protect the rest in the near future. The agreement is designed to last for 999 years, an unusually long horizon that reflects the family’s intention to make the protection effectively permanent. For a farm located in a fast-urbanising region, that legal restriction may matter more than any single owner’s promise to keep it agricultural.Stevens has been candid about the financial trade-off. He told CBC News that a developer once offered him C$16 million for the land, an offer he declined. He has also said that thinking too much about the money involved in placing land in trust could stop a farmer from doing it, explaining that he has never seen anyone take even one dollar to the grave and use it.Why the land matters beyond the familyThe protection of Wilmot Orchards has consequences that extend well beyond the Stevens family. Ontario Farmland Trust executive director Martin Straathof described the farm as a promise and a beacon of food security and sovereignty, located on the doorstep of a growing city that needs local food. The easement helps ensure that a productive farm close to a major population centre remains capable of growing fruit rather than becoming another subdivision.The decision also speaks to a wider problem in Canadian agriculture: young and beginning farmers often cannot afford land whose price has been driven up by development potential. Stevens argued that placing farmland in trust is one of the few ways a young farmer in his area might be able to buy land at a farm price, because the easement removes the development premium from the property. In that sense, the family’s action is not only about preserving their own legacy but also about keeping farming economically possible for others.The timing is important. CBC News has reported that Canada has lost millions of hectares of farmland, raising concerns about food security and the future of agriculture near expanding cities. Wilmot Orchards offers one response to that trend: rather than waiting for policy alone to protect farmland, a landowning family used a voluntary legal tool to secure its agricultural future.A growing model for farmland protectionWilmot Orchards is the 25th property protected by the Ontario Farmland Trust and its first in Durham Region. With the Stevens farm included, the trust says it has protected more than 2,700 acres across Ontario. The organisation has set a larger goal of reaching 10,000 protected acres by 2029, a target that depends on more landowners choosing similar conservation agreements.The Stevens family’s decision may encourage other farmers facing similar offers to consider easements as an option. It does not erase the financial pressures of farming, nor does it solve every challenge facing agriculture in Ontario. But it demonstrates that a farm can be treated as more than real estate waiting for a higher and better use.For now, Wilmot Orchards continues to grow apples and blueberries, welcome visitors and employ the knowledge of several generations. Its future is no longer dependent only on market pressures or the intentions of one family. Through a 999-year easement, the Stevens family has written their choice into the land itself, ensuring that this fertile corner of Ontario remains a farm rather than another development site.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2025, an Indiana appeals court let five gravel speed bumps remain on a road to a landlocked hunting property; the neighbour had installed them after raising concerns about contractors speeding near his children and dogs
articles.summary: An Indiana appeals court rules in favor of retaining five gravel speed bumps on a neighbor's easement, balancing safety and property access rights in a landlocked hunting area.
articles.body: Access easements can allow a landlocked parcel to reach a public road and are often created in deeds or other recorded instruments. The children and working dogs may use the area around the road, while those having the right to drive there could be hunters, contractors or occasional visitors. The dispute reached the Indiana Court of Appeals, which considered how far a landowner may go to slow traffic on a road subject to a neighbor’s easement.A twenty-foot easement between the Gigers and Joshua Hogue The background and legal findings come from the Indiana Court of Appeals opinion in Anthony J. Giger v. Joshua L. Hogue, issued on October 24, 2025, which affirmed the denial of an injunction to remove five gravel speed bumps from an access easement. In its opinion in Giger v. Hogue, the Indiana Court of Appeals held that speed bumps are not automatically unlawful and that their effect on an easement holder’s rights depends on whether they materially impair or unreasonably interfere with reasonable passage. Since 2006, Anthony Giger and his wife have owned an adjacent property in Nineveh, Indiana, which they use for hunting and recreational purposes. This land is officially considered to be landlocked; an easement of twenty feet in width for access through roadways and utilities has been established and it runs through some of the land acquired by Joshua Hogue in 2020. Hogue lived on the land with his wife, children and working dogs. The trial court opinion also noted intense animosity between the families and found that Hogue had obstructed the easement in different ways until 2022.Five gravel speed bumps built in 2024 It all started for Hogue in early 2024 when he observed the contractors on the neighboring property speeding down the road. According to the opinion, Hogue requested that they slow down and even put up a sign stating “slow down, children and dogs present.” With vehicles still moving at a rate which he considered too dangerous, he put up five speed bumps out of gravel. He presented two photographs as evidence. The first one showed the speed bumps to be about four inches high, while the other picture was taken after five months of putting up the speed bumps and indicated that they had worn down.Following the completion of the work by the contractors, Giger requested that the speed bumps be removed, but Hogue rejected that proposal. The Gigers filed a suit in Brown Circuit Court requesting a permanent injunction. At trial, Giger argued that the speed bumps made him speed up and slow down and created a rough ride, although he admitted that the speed bumps were not hindering him from traveling through the easement. Judge Mary Wertz rejected the request.Why Judge DeBoer treated speed bumps as a question of factThe Gigers argued that Indiana law bars interference with easements and that speed bumps are unreasonable per se. Judge DeBoer, along with Chief Judge Altice and Judge Pyle, disagreed with both claims. The panel cited Drees Co. v. Thompson from 2007, which states that a landowner may not materially impair or unreasonably interfere with an easement, distinguishing Rennaker v. Gleason from 2009, in which the removed obstacles included telephone poles, boulders, fence posts and movable piers.The ruling emphasizes that there are no cases in Indiana law that consider speed bumps unreasonable, while courts in Florida, Missouri, New York and Oregon have refused to do so. One case in particular from Oregon dating back to 1981 has been identified wherein a bump of no more than seven inches was determined not to be unreasonable interference. The panel found that whether speed bumps unreasonably impair the easement is a question of fact and affirmed the ruling.Pedestrian injury risk and speed hump evidence The court considered Hogue’s stated reason irrelevant to its decision, although research supports the general safety concerns underlying his actions. The AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety published Impact Speed and a Pedestrian’s Risk of Severe Injury or Death in 2011, drawing on federal crash data from 1994 to 1998. The research showed that the average risk of sustaining severe injuries when hit by a vehicle is 10% at 16 mph, 25% at 23 mph and 50% at 31 mph. The paper adds that the risk curves were standardized to a U.S. pedestrian struck by a car or light truck in 2007-2009, after weighting the 1994-1998 federal crash data to correct for oversampling of the most severely injured pedestrians. It also found that age mattered: a 70-year-old hit at 25 mph faced about the same risk of severe injury or death as a 30-year-old struck at 35 mph.Whether bumps lower collision rates has been tested separately. The study Installation of speed humps and pedestrian-motor vehicle collisions in Toronto, Canada: a quasi-experimental study, published in BMC Public Health, analyzed 27,827 pedestrian collisions recorded between 2000 and 2011. The collision rates per meter of road per month decreased after installation. They recommended conducting an area-wide study to ensure that the collisions have just been relocated to other streets instead of being reduced. The study covered municipal speed humps on public streets, not private gravel bumps like those in Indiana. The authors mapped the collisions across 404 classified roadways and found 1,344 crashes on 176 kilometers of roads with speed humps, with 296 fewer collisions overall after installation.What the ruling means for easement disputes The decision turns upon the findings of fact presented in court and, most notably, the testimony that the bumps did not stop Mr. Giger from entering his land. A higher or more rigid obstacle that effectively hindered any reasonable access to the plaintiff's land could also have been ordered to be cleared away. The above-mentioned study found that collision rates declined more among children than adults, with estimated reductions of 43% for children and 20% for adults. However, the research examined public roadways in Toronto, not the private gravel access road involved in the Indiana case.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Chancellor says he will cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to £800m
articles.summary: Ministers say the changes in regulations will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy.
articles.body:
The chancellor has announced plans to slash "form-filling and pointless paperwork" to save UK businesses up to £800m.

Ministers have said the proposed changes in regulations, announced ahead of John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday, will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy for businesses.

The move is part of a broader effort in the Budget to offer households and businesses more support amid rising costs.

In response to the announcement, the Conservatives said Labour had only made problems worse for businesses.

"Labour have finally admitted that endless red tape is hammering businesses and killing jobs across the country," shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said.

Healey acknowledged British firms are "fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork" eating into time and money that would be more valuable invested into their businesses.

He becomes the latest chancellor to pledge to slash red tape, which he said will allow businesses more "breathing space" to invest and create good jobs.

The changes should make compliance guidance easier, and simplify the reporting rules firms have to follow, the Treasury said.

Ministers have claimed this will save almost £800m in administrative and tariff costs.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Healey are expected to meet some business leaders on Friday at No 10 North.

Burnham said that it's unfair "pointless bureaucracy gets in the way" of hard-working people building their businesses.

"If you run a business, you want to spend your time serving your customers, creating jobs and growing your firm, not filling in unnecessary forms," Burnham said.

The government has set itself a target of cutting regulation by 25% by the end of the current Parliament.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) Chief Executive Rain Newton Smith has welcomed the plans, but said the test would be in delivering reform.

Meanwhile, the shadow chancellor argued that the unemployment act had only made "the situation worse and has created a youth jobs emergency".

"John Healey must get a grip in his Budget next week. He must back our Conservative plans to cut welfare and cut taxes so we can get Britain working again," he said.

articles.title: Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says
articles.summary: Kanishka Narayan tells the BBC that dealing with the technology requires not only regulation, but "building capability and capacity".
articles.body:
Britain cannot let aritificial intelligence be ruled by "tech bros and oligarchs", the AI minister has said.

Kanishka Narayan told the BBC's Political Thinking podcast that dealing with the technology requires not only regulation, but "building capability and capacity in the state" too.

He compared AI to the Victorian-era Industrial Revolution, but said the country needed to transition better than it did back then.

His comments were recorded the day before Barclays banking group announced it was cutting 5,000 jobs in an AI-led efficiency drive.

He was also speaking before another major AI-related development - the discovery of a cyber-security flaw affecting millions of websites , which was found with the help of AI.

Narayan, who became the UK's first cabinet minister for AI when he was appointed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July, said the scale of the technological change was "something that we haven't seen for decades and decades".

"It is comparable and in some ways exceeds the Industrial Revolution," he said, referencing the shift from a predominantly agricultural economy to industrial and manufacturing sectors between about 1750 and 1900.

The Labour MP told the BBC's Nick Robinson that Britain needed to avoid what happened in the Industrial Revolution where "the outcome as a whole was good for the country, but the transition was extremely painful for too many people".

"The fundamental thing is that the British public and democracy has to assert power rather than leave it to tech bros and oligarchs," he added.

He did not name any specific companies or tech bosses.

As well as "pulling the lever of regulation", the country needs to build AI in Britain "so you can shape the working conditions" and avoid it all being developed abroad, he said.

"We need to build technology to defend ourselves and to grow ourselves so we have leverage internationally - we're now currently totally reliant on other countries for essential bits of technology," he added.

Pointing to the capabilities of AI, he said the government recently used frontier AI models in Whitehall to check for cybersecurity issues.

"We only spent £13,000 on it - we discovered 500 new vulnerabilities. These are novel vulnerabilities that we discovered in significant areas of the public sector," Narayan said, without detailing what they were.

He also said his conversations with Chancellor John Healey had hinted at a potential AI announcement in next week's Budget, though he did not say what this was.

Narayan rejected the notion that the US and China were the only powers that matter for AI, saying the UK's AI Security Institute had seen "every US lab...coming to us" asking it to test models before deployment .

Earlier this month, Narayan warned it was likely the UK's cyber defences will at some point be breached, after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June.

He has made a series of interventions in recent weeks after an AI safety researcher went public with claims that people building the technology believed it could destroy humanity.

articles.title: In 2024, California floods washed away a private access road twice; an appeals court upheld moving the easement across a neighbour’s land but reversed an order requiring riverbank stabilization
articles.summary: A California appeals court has ruled on the complex legalities surrounding easements after floods devastated private access roads, impacting rural properties. The decision highlights the balance of rights and responsibilities between property owners in flood-prone areas.
articles.body: Roads built beside a river sit on ground that floodwater can reshape. In such a case, where the easement road is the only legal way to reach the adjacent land from the other end, all it takes is just one flood and the landowner will find themselves with legal access but no real access whatsoever. It falls to the courts to decide how to go ahead with that road and at whose cost. The problem is especially relevant for rural land with no connection to a public road, where the only access runs through an easement across a neighbor’s property. The owner of the land whose burden is to bear the easement will want the easement as narrow as possible, while the one with the easement would want a sturdy way through. A California appellate court addressed that issue after two floods destroyed the access road to a specific property.A landlocked parcel on the South Fork of the Trinity RiverThe California Court of Appeal, Third Appellate District, issued its partially published opinion in Judicial Branch of California on December 2, 2024, and modified it on January 2, 2025, without changing the judgment. Eberhard and Ursula Schneider and Karla Lane are the owners of adjacent properties on the north bank of the South Fork of the Trinity River. The Lane property is situated west of the Schneider property and would be landlocked without an express easement from the Schneider property to a county road on the east side. The easement ran over the existing road named River Road, located along the bank of the river. The flood that happened in 2002 caused damages to parts of the road. Lane filed her case in 2003 and the court in 2011 found that the easement encumbered the whole Schneider property and could be relocated to a permitted road at the southern edge of the property.The 2018 flood, the 2019 lawsuit and the trial court’s riverbank orderThe flooding in 2018 washed away the 2011 road and the Schneiders sued Lane in 2019, claiming that Lane failed to maintain the road as required by Section 845 of the Civil Code. After Lane’s motion for summary judgment based on the doctrine of res judicata in answer to their complaint was granted by the trial court, the court tried Lane’s cross-complaint. Lane offered three alternative paths farther inland, which were going to impact Schneider’s property increasingly. The court preferred the proposal made by the Schneiders themselves, since it had the least impact on their property. Under Section 845, the trial court held that Lane had to maintain the riverbank at her own expense. In Schneider v. Lane, the California Court of Appeal noted that the stabilization work would cover about 25 feet of riverbank located 30 to 50 feet from the road, with an expert estimating design costs of up to $250,000 and construction costs of up to $1 million.Why the panel reversed the stabilization order under Civil Code section 845Appeals were taken by all. The Acting Presiding Judge delivered for the court, which consisted of Judge Hull, Judge Krause and Judge Mesiwala. This decision affirmed in part and reversed in part. It found that the relocation was justified because the 2011 decision had already established that the easement can be moved. The panel reversed the order requiring riverbank stabilization. Civil Code section 845 tells an easement owner to “maintain it in repair,” and the panel reads that as keeping the easement itself in good and sound condition. The statute does not mandate that the owner build a new improvement apart from the right-of-way. The decision further states that there had been no reported California case law concerning whether the owner has the obligation to stabilize the adjacent riverbank. Both parties paid their own expenses on appeal.What flood modelling and streambank monitoring add to the disputeXingying Huang and Daniel Swain published Climate change is increasing the risk of a California megaflood in Science Advances on August 12, 2022, and their modeling suggests that climate change may have already roughly doubled the likelihood of an event capable of catastrophic flooding in the state. The authors’ simulations projected that a megaflood would bring much more rainfall than the historical 1861-62 event, with peak runoff up to five times greater than the 1996 to 2005 baseline. The authors note that the risk remains high even under a 2°C warming scenario.On the cost side, the study Quantifying Effectiveness of Streambank Stabilization Practices on Cedar River, Nebraska, published in Water, tracked 18 stabilized streambanks using aerial images from 1993 to 2016. Jetties succeeded in 70% of cases, produced the greatest deposition and were the most cost-effective approach. The authors identified gravel beaches and retaining walls as alternative shoreline protections, but said specific recommendations and use conditions still need to be defined. Six practices, among which there were jetties, rock vanes and retaining walls were considered. The study concluded that jetties had the highest percentage of success (70%) and the greatest amount of deposition, being the most cost-effective choice.What the ruling leaves in place for easement holders and neighboursThis ruling grants neither complete freedom of movement to easement owners nor unlimited rights for such movements. According to its ruling in Schneider v. Lane, the California Court of Appeal, Third Appellate District, stated that if the relocation of an easement is to be done, the court is supposed to ensure that the new route poses a minimum burden to the landowner in question. There might even be a provision for compensation in equity in the case of extra burden posed on the property. This court did not grant any form of compensation in this case, as the route selected was the least burdensome on the property of Schneiders, with it being said that the routes proposed by Lane called for compensation to be granted to her.You use AI every day. articles.title: Book Week NI: What had people turning pages and turning up the volume this year?
articles.summary: Thrillers, self-help books and Harry Potter were the big winners for readers from Libraries NI data.
articles.body:
Thrillers, self-help books and Harry Potter were among the favourites for readers in Northern Ireland this year, according to Libraries NI.

For those who prefered to listen to their fiction, Freida McFadden had eight of her titles featuring in the top 10 adult fiction audiobooks borrowed.

Jillian McFrederick from Libraries NI said books with "short chapters" and "catchy, racy" themes seemed to be most popular.

But when it came to younger readers, there was little change with Harry Potter continuing to be popular - almost 30 years after the release of the first book.

This week marks Book Week - a joint initiative between BBC NI and Libraries NI and celebrates books, reading and libraries and everything that they make possible.

The data provided by Libraries NI covers a 12-month period from 1 October 2025 to 30 September 2026.

So, which audio books have been the most popular?

Audiobooks led the way this year with more downloads than physical book loans.

The Housemaid by McFadden was the most listened to, with only Romantasy favourite Fourth Wing by Rebecca Yarros and The Pumpkin Spiced Café by Laurie Gilmore breaking McFadden's hold on the chart.

When it came to non-fiction, those listening seem focused on personal development.

A best-selling title by Mark Manson, The Subtle Art of not Giving a ... (Google the rest if you wish), topped the non-fiction section, while Atomic Habits and 101 Essays That Will Change the Way You Think followed closely behind.

Meanwhile, for younger listeners, the Harry Potter series remained the standout success with all seven books from the series making it into the top 10.

Other favourites included classic titles such as Matilda by Roald Dahl, and Diary of a Wimpy Kid by Jeff Kinney.

There is still a strong demand for physicals

The Housemaid also topped the charts when it came to physical loans, with the title being borrowed more than 3,000 times.

McFrederick said the release of the movie adaptation, starring Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfield in 2025, had brought a whole new audience to McFadden's work.

Niall Williams' historical fiction book based in 1960s Ireland, Time of the Child, came close to beating McFadden with only 15 loans behind.

When it came to non-fiction, global best-seller, The Let Them Theory by Mel Robbins came first, slightly ahead of Nobody's Girl by Virginia Roberts Giuffre.

The wider top five reflected variety from self improvement to baking, including Mary Berry's very best recipes.

Variety continued for junior readers. A Belfast Fairytale led the fiction category with nearly 3,000 loans and the Guinness World Records 2026 took the lead in non-fiction.

Ebooks showed library users were split between very different reading habits over the last year.

In fiction, readers gravitated towards page turners from authors like Virginia Evans with The Correspondent claiming top spot.

Richard Osman showed a true favourite with three of the top 10 being written by him.

Andy Weir's Project Hail Mary also proved popular following a movie adaption earlier this year.

For non-fiction, self-help was a clear winner. Again, Mel Robbin's The Let Them Theory came first, with more than 2,000 loans.

McFrederick said the book "struck a chord with people because they're all so stressed and so anxious".

Other popular self-help books were also in the top five including The Psychology of Money and The Courage to be Disliked .

Among younger readers, the magic around the Harry Potter series continued with more than 1,500 loans in fiction.

Junior non-fiction interests ranged from The Wimpy Kid Movie Diary, Historical Royal Palaces: Ghost in the Walls and 101 Amazing Harry Potter Facts among the most borrowed eBooks.

articles.title: In 1954, an Alabama farmer found a piece of a meteorite on a dirt road; he sold it for enough to buy a farm and a car, but the exact price was never reported
articles.summary: In 1954, an Alabama farmer found a meteorite on a dirt road, selling it for enough to buy a house and a car. Explore the puzzling stories of two meteorite discoveries linked to the famous Sylacauga fall.
articles.body: Most stony meteorites give little warning beyond a bright fireball and a series of sonic booms. In the following minutes, questions will start arising about what landed and where. Once such a meteoroid starts breaking down in the upper atmosphere, the resulting chunks do not stay together and scatter all around, landing on rooftops, in fields and even in the middle of the road. It all depends on the finder and their ability to determine the significance of the find. Such instances were recorded twice in the famous fall in the Southern United States and it is also the same case where there is not a single piece of financial information revealed.The Hodges stone and the fireball over Oak Grove The Encyclopedia of Alabama records that a meteorite crashed through the roof of a home near Sylacauga, in Talladega County, on November 30, 1954 and struck resident Ann E. Hodges. The rock reportedly weighed about eight and a half pounds and is now on display at the Alabama Museum of Natural History in Tuscaloosa. The minerals database Mindat suggests that the rock first hit a radio console and then struck Mrs. Hodges. Mindat gives the stone’s weight as 3.86 kilograms, while the combined weight of the two stones is reported as 5.54 kilograms. It categorizes it as a chondrite of the H4 type. Mindat lists the fall time as 12:46 hours on November 30, 1954. The ownership of the meteorite was a point of conflict as well. While the encyclopedia claims that it was only after the intervention of the congressman, Kenneth Roberts, that the stone was returned to the state, Alabama Living magazine claims that the landlady of the Hodges returned it to the Hodges family in 1955 for $500.Julius Kempis McKinney and the second stone The second stone was discovered by Julius Kempis McKinney, a local farmer who, the Encyclopedia of Alabama says, found it on a dirt road on December 1, 1954, when his mules refused to move because of the black rock. He sold the piece through a lawyer and it went to the Smithsonian Institution, for enough money to buy a small farm and a used car.There are different stories of the discovery. One of them says that he brought the stone to the postman, who was the only government representative he trusted. Another story states that he put the stone aside and came back home in the evening, having heard about the stone of the Hodges. Mindat lists the McKinney stone’s weight as 1.68 kilograms. The postman and McKinney concluded that there must be a connection between the rock and the Hodges stone and it could be valuable. The information can be found on the Weekly Recess website.A sale to the Smithsonian whose price was never reportedAlabama Living reports that the sum was never revealed and the Weekly Recess and Bizzarro Bazar websites likewise give no figure for the amount. The Encyclopedia of Alabama describes McKinney as probably the only major figure in the story to claim a satisfactory ending. Smithsonian magazine reports that McKinney’s stone is in the collections of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, where it is on view. Hodges donated her stone to the Alabama Museum of Natural History in 1956, after the ownership dispute left her unable to find a buyer, according to Sky at Night Magazine.What a 2019 NASA analysis says about meteorite strikes on people and buildingsThe NASA analysis, Kinetic Damage from Meteorites, presented as a poster at the 2019 Planetary Defense Conference, describes the Sylacauga stone as a 4-kilogram meteorite that indirectly hit Hodges. In addition, a 4-gram stone falling onto a young boy is recorded for the 1992 Mbale fall; neither incident caused death. The poster adds that fragments on the order of 0.1 kilograms may be enough to cause serious human injury or death and it cites Halliday et al.’s 1985 estimate that a person is struck by a meteorite roughly once a decade, most likely by a gram-sized piece. A second study,The fall, recovery, classification, and initial characterization of the Hamburg, Michigan H4 chondrite, published in Meteoritics & Planetary Science, examined a stone from the 2018 Michigan fall that belongs to the same H4 group as the Sylacauga stones.Why the two Sylacauga stones ended so differentlyThe same NASA poster also lists 48 meteorites found in North America between 1962 and 2016, of which 23 fell on roofs or buildings and three on cars. In other words, a meteorite striking a building is not unusual, but one striking a person, as happened to Hodges, remains extremely rare. McKinney’s good fortune lay in recognizing that the rock might be valuable and acting on it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Clarity demanded from Guernsey's government on airline's purpose
articles.summary: The airline's CEO said it is difficult to balance high costs and low air fares within its mandate.
articles.body:
The chief executive officer of Aurigny hopes for clarity on what the airline's purpose should be in the future.

Nico Bezuidenhout held briefings this week for Guernsey deputies, following projections of a £9.7m loss in 2026 with a further £5.7m loss next year.

Bezuidenhout said it has been difficult to balance keeping airfares down and increasing reliability alongside record high fuel prices and competition.

The Committee for Economic Development has been approached for comment.

The airline's mandate from the government is to break-even, which Bezuidenhout said they were "striving towards" but that there was a "cost to bear" when it comes to reliable air travel.

"Whether that cost must be borne by the states or by the paying public is an open debate and an open question

"It becomes a matter of clarity of purpose going forward" he added.

The Air Policy Framework, which defines the strategic roles and responsibilities or the airline will be presented and debated by the States early next year.

Bezuidenhout said that a "competitive, subsidised environment" in the new Heathrow route "adds an additional burden and imbalance to that equation."

Despite Aurigny receiving bailouts from the government when it made losses, the CEO said:

"I'd way rather prefer to have an upfront subsidy that I can pass through into the hands of the residents of Guernsey than to receive an after-the-fact compensation for losses suffered".

Other cost saving possibilities mentioned by Bezuidenhout included reframing airport costs and airport charges:

"We've seen that that's been used where carriers might have been subsidised through airport fees".

articles.title: In 2016, carp overran Idaho’s 100-acre Bruneau Dunes Pond, outcompeting bass; rotenone cleared them, 2,200 fish were restocked, and a 2019 survey found no carp
articles.summary: Discover how Idaho Fish and Game successfully eradicated invasive common carp from Bruneau Lake, allowing for the restoration of a thriving fishing ecosystem. Learn about the methods used, the challenges faced, and the positive results of their measurements.
articles.body: Common carp can take over a small fishing pond, muddying the water and outcompeting bass and bluegill. At Bruneau Dunes State Park in Idaho, managers decided the fix was to remove every fish and start over. In October 2016, Idaho Fish and Game treated the 100-acre pond with rotenone, restocked it and surveyed it again in July 2019.Common carp in Bruneau Dunes PondIdaho Fish and Game’s 2019 report describes Bruneau Dunes Pond, inside Bruneau Dunes State Park, as a popular fishing spot known for big bass and bluegill until it became infested with common carp. According to the report, the carp reproduced quickly and outcompeted the bass and bluegill. In a November 2016 press release, Idaho Fish and Game reported that most bass in Bruneau Dunes Pond were undersized, measuring around 8 inches, while only one reached 20 inches. This observation was taken by the agency to mean that carp is affecting their growth.Rotenone was applied from two crop-duster planesIdaho Fish and Game launched the operation in October 2016 by using the fish toxin rotenone on the surface of the 100-acre pond. The agency's 2016 release states that two crop duster planes from a Nampa company undertook the task. Hundreds of dead carp were removed and taken either to a landfill or a rendering plant in Hagerman. Because rotenone is nonselective, it also killed the bass and bluegill that remained in the pond. Before the operation, fish were electrofished in the pond and moved to another nearby pond. Doug Megargle, regional fishery manager, warned that a total kill cannot be guaranteed. Idaho Fish and Game further stated that rotenone rapidly degrades in sunlight and therefore, the pond will again be able to support fish within a week or two.Restocking with 2,000 bluegill in 2017 and 200 bass in 2018According to the 2019 report, the biologists restocked the pond with 2,000 bluegill in 2017 and 200 bass in 2018. This amounts to 2,200 fish altogether. The 2016 restocking estimate predicted that the pond would be restored in a period of three to five years and would contain plenty of bluegills and trophy largemouths.The July 2019 electrofishing survey and what it foundIn July 2019, regional fisheries biologist Joe Thiessen conducted an electrofishing survey, with the boat working the shoreline for 30 minutes at a time. The July 2019 survey observed no carp, bluegill that were growing well and spawning and signs that a bass population was re-establishing. That was a single survey three years after treatment and Idaho Fish and Game said it would keep monitoring the fishery. Thiessen said young-of-year bluegill from 2018 had grown 3 to 4 inches, exceeding growth rates reported in Midwest states. No bass above 20 inches were seen, though several between 14 and 18 inches were caught, so the bass population may still be limited.What research says about removing carpTwo published studies show what carp can do to aquatic plants and what removing them can and cannot fix. A 2016 study in Global Change Biology, Biological invasion by a benthivorous fish reduced the cover and species richness of aquatic plants in most lakes of a large North American ecoregion, found that submersed plant cover fell below 10 percent and species richness was cut in half in lakes where carp biomass exceeded 190 kilograms per hectare, a result from the lakes studied rather than a universal threshold. It estimated that carp biomass exceeded that level in a majority of Great Plains lakes and a large portion of Eastern Temperate Forests lakes.A 2015 study by Przemyslaw Bajer and Peter Sorensen, published in Hydrobiologia, tracked a thermally stratified lake while carp biomass was cut from 300 to 40 kilograms per hectare. Vegetation density and springtime water clarity rose, but summer clarity did not improve and carp removal had no apparent effect on total phosphorus.What the evidence suggests for waters like Bruneau Dunes PondThe findings suggest that keeping carp biomass below levels associated with ecological damage could support restoration, although the right target may vary with each water’s conditions. Idaho went a step further by removing all of the carp. The 2015 study is a reminder that removal does not fix everything, so water quality may recover more slowly than the plants.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2022, a Texas couple found their vacant rental house stripped of its air conditioner, copper wiring and plumbing; Allstate denied the claim, and a 2025 appeals court upheld the ruling for the insurer
articles.summary: In a landmark case, a Texas couple faced insurance denial from Allstate after their rental property was stripped of valuable components. Learn how the court ruled on the implications of vacancy on insurance claims.
articles.body: On paper, buying a home to rent out is straightforward: find a tenant, fix up the property and start collecting rent. The insurance policy normally sits in a drawer until something goes wrong. At that point, owners often discover that rental property coverage comes with restrictions on how the building is used. Insuring a home with no occupants differs greatly from insuring one with occupants, and the difference can be costly.That is what one Texas couple found in 2022. In 2021, Bradley and Crystal Childers bought an investment property in Lufkin, insured it with Allstate Indemnity Company and began renovations while looking for a tenant. In March 2022, the house was stripped of its air conditioning equipment, copper wiring and plumbing. The insurer rejected the claim, and in February 2025 the Fifth Circuit, a US federal appeals court, upheld a finding in its favour. The key question was whether the residence had been vacant for more than 60 consecutive days before the theft, a dispute that turned on the meaning of two everyday terms.What the policy coveredThe Childerses held what Allstate called a Landlords Package Policy, and two of its provisions mattered, according to the Fifth Circuit’s opinion. One covered damage to the exterior of a structure caused by a burglar breaking in, but only if the house was complete and had not been vacant or unoccupied for more than 60 consecutive days before the loss. The other covered fire damage caused by vandalism, with the same 60-day condition. Both protections would disappear if a property sat vacant or unoccupied long enough.Bradley’s grandparents drove past on 29 March 2022 and saw that the pad for a new air conditioning unit had been stripped. The couple rushed over and found the house burgled and vandalised. Police lifted a fingerprint, but nobody was ever identified. Crystal later testified that Allstate first told her the policy would pay but a few days later said the claim was refused because it believed the property had been vacant or unoccupied for more than 60 consecutive days. The couple sued in Texas state court, and the insurer moved the case to federal court.How the case came togetherAfter the dispute began, the insurer sent written requests asking the couple to confirm a few basic facts, such as whether they had lived at the house, whether it was inhabited, and whether a tenant had ever stayed there. The Childerses never responded. Under federal court rules, requests left unanswered are treated as admitted, and the judge accepted the statements as true.Later, when the insurer asked for summary judgment, a ruling without a full trial when the key facts are not genuinely in dispute, Crystal filed an affidavit describing the Lufkin house as the couple’s home and saying they lived there. That conflicted with her earlier sworn testimony. In her deposition, she had said the house was bought as a rental, that the couple had lived in Wells, Texas, for six years, and that nobody had lived at the Lufkin property since the purchase. The trial judge struck the affidavit paragraph as a sham, meaning a later statement that contradicts earlier sworn evidence without explanation, and the appeals court said that was within the judge’s discretion.The couple argued that Lufkin was a secondary residence and the policy was ambiguous on the matter. The court was not convinced. It was a landlord's insurance, it said, which presupposes that the owners reside someplace else. Its description of the insured premises specified the building at the stated address rather than the owners’ personal house.Vacant vs. unoccupiedUnder Texas law, the two terms are not the same. A property is vacant when it has no furnishings of any real use, so a house with furniture is not vacant. The Lufkin property still had vanities, dressers and mirrors inside, so the insurer could not win on the vacancy argument alone.But occupancy is about people, not belongings. A house is occupied when people regularly use it as a place to live, and it is unoccupied when they do not. Furniture does not change that. The exclusion applied to properties that were vacant or unoccupied, and Crystal’s own testimony indicated that nobody had lived in the house for at least 60 days before the loss, so one word was sufficient. A federal court cannot redefine a term contrary to what the Texas Supreme Court has previously said.Owners who disagree with an insurer’s assessment have options. The Texas Department of Insurance recommends that policyholders explain to the company why they disagree and supply supporting documents such as a contractor’s estimate. If that does not work, many policies provide an appraisal procedure, and policyholders can also file a complaint with the department, request mediation, or go to court. That advice is meant for homeowners and renters, so landlords should review their own policy’s handling of disputes.The case hinged on facts the couple could not change by the time it reached court. The appeals court did not designate its opinion for publication, which typically means it is not binding precedent. Nevertheless, it shows how Texas courts interpret these terms and how quickly a 60-day gap can decide a claim.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Can't drive into future looking at rearview mirror': India calls for urgent UNSC reforms
articles.summary: India has called for urgent reforms to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), warning that its 80-year-old structure is struggling to address some of
articles.body: India has called for urgent reforms to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), warning that its 80-year-old structure is struggling to address some of the world’s gravest conflicts. New Delhi said the Council’s composition must reflect present-day global realities, arguing that its post-Second World War framework no longer adequately represents the international community.According to news agency PTI, India’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, said on Thursday that the authority inherited from the Second World War could no longer compensate for the Council’s lack of representative membership.“The cost is already visible. Eighty years on, the Organisation is struggling to deliver peace and reconciliation in some of the gravest conflicts before the Council,” Parvathaneni said while addressing the UN General Assembly on equitable representation and an expansion of the Security Council.He added that “the authority derived from a victory eight decades ago cannot compensate for the deficit in legitimacy of an unrepresentative Security Council today.”The Indian envoy argued that 1945, when the UN was established after the Second World War, could not remain the sole reference point for global governance.“No war, especially one that took place over 80 years ago, should determine today’s state of the world,” he said.“History can be a guide for what not to do. It cannot determine today’s choices for what needs to be done to face contemporary challenges. We cannot reasonably drive into the future by constantly looking at the rearview mirror,” he added.Parvathaneni also highlighted India’s contribution to the World Wars, arguing that the sacrifices of several nations had not received adequate recognition in the post-war international order.“An organisation crafted of the victors, for the victors and by the victors did not, obviously, care to include the concerns of the victims,” he said, calling for the Security Council to evolve “for the sake of its own relevance”.According to PTI, he noted that around 2.5 million Indians participated in the Second World War, with approximately 90,000 dying in military service. He also referred to the Bengal famine, which he attributed to colonial wartime policies.India further pointed to the under-representation of Asia-Pacific, Africa and Latin America. The Asia-Pacific region accounts for more than 60 per cent of the world’s population but has only one permanent seat on the Council, alongside a fluctuating elected representation.“Reform is not the settlement of old scores. It is an investment in a Council that all Member States can trust, and which would be stronger as a result,” Parvathaneni said.The 15-member UNSC comprises five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — with veto powers, alongside 10 elected members serving two-year terms.India supports expanding both permanent and non-permanent membership, arguing that changes limited to elected seats would leave the central imbalance intact.Criticising the pace of negotiations, Parvathaneni said, “That is not negotiation; it is merely perpetuation of status quo.”He added, “Convergences are not consensus, and the search for a lowest common denominator must not become an excuse for cosmetically tinkering with the existing structure while calling it reform.”India also maintained that any permanent membership expansion must address the veto question fairly. “A two-tier permanent membership would only institutionalise inequality,” he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: €50 million for a Monet: ‘Iris’ sets French auction record after decades in hiding
articles.summary: A monumental painting titled Iris by french impressionist artist Claude Monet sold for 50 million euros ($56 million), including buyer fees, at an auction
articles.body: A monumental painting titled Iris by french impressionist artist Claude Monet sold for 50 million euros ($56 million), including buyer fees, at an auction in Paris on Thursday, setting a record for the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction in France.Measuring 1.60 metres in height and 1.80 metres in width, the painting had remained inside the Paris mansion of the billionaire Schlumberger family and was known publicly only through a black-and-white photograph, according to yahoo.com.According to Thomas Bompard, co-head of Sotheby's France's modern and contemporary art department, the artwork was acquired by Jeanne Schlumberger (1889–1983).Before the auction, Sotheby's had estimated its value at between 22 million and 30 million euros. The auction house described this as the highest estimate ever assigned to a painting being offered at auction in France.Monet created Iris during the later years of his life, adding to the significance of the work.Other Monet paintings featured in the auctionThree additional paintings by Monet were included in the Sotheby's sale. Among them was saule pleureur (weeping willow), which carried an estimated price of between 9 million and 12 million euros.The auction coincides with the centenary year of monet's death on December 5, 1926. His legacy is being commemorated in Paris through two exhibitions, Monet, painting time and stories of landscapes, from monet to hockney.Meanwhile, three paintings by Paul cezanne, designated as national treasures, were withdrawn from the Sotheby's auction just hours before it began. The decision was taken to facilitate their potential return to the artist's hometown of aix-en-provence, the auction house said.The withdrawal followed an agreement between the paintings' current owners and the city of aix-en-provence. With support from France's culture ministry, the city is exploring the possibility of acquiring the artworks.Christie's paris auction generates 41.6 million eurosA separate auction organised by Christie's in Paris on Thursday featured 26 artworks, including two paintings by Monet.Bord des falaises à pourville sold for 12.7 million euros, while Trois pots de tulipes fetched 3.1 million euros.Other notable sales included pierre-auguste Renoir's jeunes filles au bord de la mer, which went for 5.8 million euros, and pablo picasso's nature morte au gruyère, which sold for 3 million euros.Christie's reported total proceeds of 41.6 million euros, inclusive of buyer fees, from the auction.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Disgrace at so many levels': Shashi Tharoor reacts to removal of Raihan Vadra's photos from exhibition
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Senior Congress leader Shashi Tharoor on Friday criticised the removal of photographs from Raihan Vadra's exhibition at Bikaner House in New
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Senior Congress leader Shashi Tharoor on Friday criticised the removal of photographs from Raihan Vadra's exhibition at Bikaner House in New Delhi, saying the move had damaged India's global reputation as a freedom-loving democracy and raised serious concerns over freedom of expression.In a post on X, Tharoor described the incident as a "disgrace at so many levels", arguing that photographs documenting protest demonstrations depicted events and did not necessarily convey political positions."This is a disgrace at so many levels," Thiruvananthapuram MP said, listing his objections to the decision to remove the photographs from the exhibition, "No Idea Is Final".He said the images documented events that had already received widespread public and media attention, questioning why photographs of demonstrations should be considered political content simply because they depicted protests."The images are of events that have already been burned into the public consciousness, and many of the photos would have echoed similar images that the public has already seen in the media and online," Tharoor said, adding that "While Bikaner House is free to have a policy against political stands, photographs of a protest demonstration are a depiction of an event and not political in themselves; they would almost certainly have passed muster had the matter been brought to a court as an issue of freedom of expression."He further alleged that the decision had hurt India's international image."And worst of all, this censorship has driven one more nail into the coffin of India's global reputation as a freedom-loving democracy," the Congress MP said.Tharoor also pointed out that the controversy had brought significant attention to Raihan Vadra's photographic work, potentially exposing it to a much wider audience than the exhibition would otherwise have reached."Anyway, the publicity this episode has received will have reached a far larger audience, in Delhi and worldwide, than the exhibition itself might have, had it been allowed to proceed undisturbed. I thank heavy-handed officials for giving a well-deserved boost to the photographic talents and career of Raihan Vadra," Tharoor said.The row began after Raihan Vadra, son of Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, alleged that Bikaner House management had asked him to remove several photographs from his exhibition shortly before its scheduled opening. According to him, the images included photographs documenting student protests and two pictures of the Indian national flag.The Bikaner House Management Society said certain photographs did not comply with its policy and that their removal had been requested. It maintained that photographs meeting the venue's guidelines continued to be displayed.The incident sparked a political confrontation, with Congress leaders criticising the decision as an infringement on artistic expression, while the BJP maintained that exhibitions must follow the venue's rules.Amid the controversy, Keralam chief minister VD Satheesan offered to host the exhibition in its entirety, saying the state would be proud to welcome “No Idea Is Final”, with "no exclusions, no exceptions".However, Kerala BJP president Rajeev Chandrasekhar questioned the offer, alleging preferential treatment for Raihan Vadra and asking whether ordinary young people received similar attention to their rights and work.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: SRINAGAR: A 45-year-old woman allegedly set on fire by her stepson inside their house in Udhampur on Wednesday evening succumbed to her burn injuries at Government Medical College in Jammu, police said.Police identified the woman as Sushma Devi, wife of Keshav Verma and a resident of Housing Colony in Udhampur.She suffered burns over around 70% of her body after her stepson, Moksh Verma, allegedly poured diesel on her and set her ablaze at their residence.The police said Verma, around 30, has been arrested and is being questioned.Visuals of the incident have surfaced. In a video clip, the woman can be seen engulfed in flames, screaming for help and attempting to run out of the house as neighbours rush to her rescue and try to extinguish the fire.Preliminary investigation suggested that the stepson had allegedly been threatening her for the past few months, a police official said, requesting anonymity.The official added that CCTV footage of the incident was available.Stay updated with the latest Srinagar news. articles.summary: New Zealand vs. India 2nd T20I prediction, team news, pitch report and betting tips. Get pre-match analysis, key players, odds and more.
articles.body:
New Zealand have two days to fix a problem that 225 runs could not hide. They host India in the second T20I at Hagley Oval on Saturday, trailing 1-0 in the five-match series after a four-wicket defeat.

Glenn Phillips struck 82 not out from 40 balls and Finn Allen added 45 from 24, yet Sanju Samson's 67 from 33 and a 93-run opening stand with Abhishek Sharma put the chase in India's hands.

Mitchell Santner and Michael Bracewell dragged the contest back in the middle overs, but Shreyas Iyer's 42 and Naman Dhi's unbeaten 42 from 15 balls finished it with two balls to spare.

The hosts must now find a way through India's top order, and they will have to do it against a side that won without the rested Jasprit Bumrah.

New Zealand vs. India 1st T20I prediction: Who will win?

New Zealand have the better case to level the series at Hagley Oval on Saturday. They scored 225 for 4 and lost by two balls, with Allen dropping a sitter at long-on that let Iyer off on 27.

Their new-ball bowlers conceded 48 in two overs and sent down four wides in the first five, and those errors are correctable.

India, meanwhile, are still adjusting after a long flight, and their bowling looked thin. Bhuvneshwar Kumar went for 49 and Axar Patel for 51, and New Zealand hit 67 off the last 30 balls.

Glenn Phillips and Allen will fancy another big total on a ground they now know well.

articles.title: Jaguar Type 01: What JLR wanted to get right inside the cabin
articles.summary: Few cars started as much debate recently as the Jaguar Type 00 concept.
articles.body: Few cars started as much debate recently as the Jaguar Type 00 concept. It was unveiled in late 2024 and its angular look and bare-bones interior got everyone talking, raising questions about whether it was too much of a break from tradition. Fast forward to 2026, things have turned around for the Type 01, which is now getting serious love for its standout design. We recently spoke with JLR’s Chief Designer of Materiality, Mary Crisp, and Chief Designer of Interior, Tom Holden, to dissect the cabin design, the materials they picked, and the ideas driving the new layout.Speaking about the Type 01’s interior, Mary Crisp, Chief Designer, Materiality at JLR, said sustainability was considered across every material, from its composition to how it could be recycled. The team calls this approach “material hygiene” and works closely with JLR’s sustainability team to assess its choices.The cabin uses lightweight carpet made from recycled polyester, while the stowage areas feature recycled felt without adhesives. The latter also avoids flocking, which Crisp described as a microplastic. Weight was another consideration, given the car’s electric powertrain.“Being an EV it's vitally important we can contribute to bringing down the overall weight of the vehicle,” she said.Luxury without adding more materialsCrisp said luxury did not mean adding more materials or ornamentation. Instead, the cabin combines layered colours, textured seat fabrics and distinctive flooring to create warmth.One of the standout elements is a brass-inspired finish, developed from experiments with artists and makers. It takes the form of anodised, embossed aluminium running along the top of the doors and the central spine. The choice of materials also extends to the door panels, which use Ultrafabrics’ Neograin product to create a continuous surface without conventional stitching. However, leather seats will remain available as an option. “We really feel like there are materials other than leather that are luxurious,” Crisp said.A different approach to technologyTom Holden, Chief Designer, Interior at JLR, said the team deliberately avoided following technology trends simply for the sake of adding features. Instead, it focused on how drivers would interact with the car and what information they needed.“We didn't want to just offer tech for the sake of tech's sake in a sort of arms race if you like,” he said. The aim was to create a driver-focused experience, with essential information readily available and other digital content remaining in the background until needed. Holden said achieving clean, uninterrupted surfaces was one of the biggest challenges. While this was a feature of some of Jaguar’s classic models, modern vehicle regulations, including side-impact requirements, made it harder to achieve.“One of the hardest things to do, which may appear as one of the most simple, it's just getting that continuous flow of beautiful clean surfaces through the car,” he said.Bringing back the classic Jaguar driving positionHolden said the driving position was central to recreating the feel of older Jaguars. The driver sits low in the cabin, with a slim dashboard and a high central spine helping create an enclosed feel. “You sit very low in this car,” he said.Textiles flowing from the floor into the door panels further contribute to the cabin’s wraparound design, bringing together the material choices and layout to create a distinct driving environment.
